title: Live with them in kindness
hookLine: live with your wives in kindness, even when you dislike something (4:19)

cards: It's the dishes. Or the way they load the dishwasher. Or the phone at dinner, the late replies, the thing they always say at family gatherings.
Share a home with someone long enough and a list can start. Most of the items are small. Some aren't.
And the list can grow louder than everything else about the person. An-Nisa has a verse for exactly that moment, plain and practical.

teach.b: Verse 19 starts by forbidding something commentators say was done in Arabia before Islam: when a man died, his heirs could treat his widow as part of the estate and control whom she married.
The verse says no: it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, and don't press them to give back what you gave them. Then it turns to marriage itself.
In Pickthall's words: "But consort with them in kindness, for if ye hate them it may happen that ye hate a thing wherein Allah hath placed much good."
The Arabic is 'ashiruhunna bil-ma'ruf. 'Ashara means to live together closely, as companions. Bil-ma'ruf: with the good everyone recognizes, the same ma'ruf as in calling to good.
Not a special religious kindness, just the ordinary decency any neighbor would know.

teach.h: DISLIKE, AND MUCH GOOD IN IT
teach.b: Then the surprise: if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which God has placed much good. The verse expects dislike. It doesn't pretend a marriage is free of it.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim puts it in household terms: a believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another.

teach.h: THE BEST OF YOU TO YOUR FAMILY
teach.b: And a hadith in Tirmidhi reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family.
Some commentators apply the verse's principle to both spouses. The list is real. The verse simply asks you to keep reading past it, to the good on the other page.

how: Muslims cite 4:19 and the hadith 'the best of you are the best to their families' in marriage sermons and counseling, as the basis for treating a spouse with recognized kindness and fairness.

o: a formal contract that ends a marriage
to keep a careful record of someone's faults
to live closely together, as companions

games.q: live with them in kindness — tap the pairs.

s: 4:19 assumes a good marriage has no dislike in it
it expects dislike, and says there may be much good in what you dislike.
the verse forbids inheriting women against their will
commentators say it ended a practice of treating widows as part of an estate.
ma'ruf here means a special religious kindness
it's the recognized good, the decency anyone would know.

games.q: you're annoyed with your spouse over a habit that won't change. what does the hadith in Sahih Muslim say?
o: tell everyone, so they'll take your side.
if you dislike one trait, you'll be pleased with another.
keep reminding them until they stop.
games.why: look for the other trait, the one you're pleased with. the hadith puts 4:19 into household terms.

practice: Think of someone you live with, or someone close: a spouse, a parent, a roommate, a sibling. Let one complaint about them come up, and don't push it away; it's real.
Then find one good thing in them, something you'd miss if they were gone, then a second, until the complaint is no longer the only thing in the room.

wordCard.voice: 'Ashara, to live together closely, as companions. 'Ashiruhunna bil-ma'ruf, from 4:19: even when you dislike something, there may be much good in it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and live with them in kindness, with the recognized good (4:19).

carryVoice: Your line: kindness at home. There may be much good in what you dislike. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: But consort with them in kindness, for if ye hate them it may happen that ye hate a thing wherein Allah hath placed much good.
